meta.title: Nu:Time™ — time and location reimagined
meta.description: Nu:Time (刻时 Ke-Shi) is an open standard for time and place: one clock for the whole planet, a decimal day of 10 gongs, 100 kè, 1,000 beats and 100,000 ticks, and a single unit — the kè — that measures both when and where.

hero.eyebrow: The Nu:Time Standard · 刻时 Ke-Shi
hero.title: time and location reimagined.
hero.sub: One clock for the whole planet connecting time and space. Measuring both when and where you are on Earth.
hero.dayBar: Today at your location, in universal Nu:Time
hero.dialHint:
Nu:Time is the same for everyone — no matter where you are. Unlike a regular clock, the four coordinates on the Nu:Time clock face rotate to match your location, keeping a fixed reference to the Prime Meridian in Greenwich.

Solar noon is always at the top of the clock and as the Sun moves across the sky, three hands mark the passage of time: the Red hand completes one revolution per day, the Blue hand one revolution every gong, and the Gold hand one revolution every beat, marking the passing ticks.

time.title: Time reimagined.
time.lead: Nu:Time is the same for everyone — no matter where you are. Where you're located no longer changes what time it is.

points.title: Universal time
points.text: It's a global world. Shanghai, Delhi, Paris and New York use the same time. Meetings, flights and markets all use the same time.

points.title: No date line
points.text: The universal day turns over once, at the same time, for everyone. No jumping back and forth days in the mid-Pacific, and no more two Tuesdays.

points.title: Your place in the sun
points.text: Your distance from the Prime Meridian in Greenwich brings the sun overhead either earlier or later, but it's always the same universal time, all the time.

points.title: Your watch, your way
points.text: Just like the watch face above, Nu:Time devices can show your local solar day and where the sun is overhead. Universal and local time are never mixed up.

how.title: The whole system fits on one line.
how.lead: Every unit is a power of ten. Every display reads the same way — gong : beat : tick.

cards.text: A tenth of the day and longer than a traditional hour: the first field of every Nu:Time reading.
One thousandth of the day: long enough to be meaningful, short enough for a meeting.
Close to a resting heartbeat. The last field of every Nu:Time reading.
With 100 Kè in a day and 100 in a circle, Kè is the bridge between time and place.

ke.title: Kè: one unit for when and where.
ke.lead: A full day is 100 kè. A full circle is 100 kè. So the Earth's rotation and the rotation of the four coordinates on the Nu:Time clock face are the same — and time zones disappear.

facts.text: 0 to 50 kè east or west of the Prime Meridian
0 to 25 kè north or south of the Equator

geometry.title: A new era of geometry.
geometry.lead: Degrees were Babylon's choice. Radians are a mathematician's. The 100-kè circle speaks the same language as your watch and your map — and makes geometry more intuitive.
geometry.trig:
sin 25 kè = 1, cos 50 kè = −1, sin 75 kè = −1 and cos 100 kè = 1.

A wave that repeats daily has a period of exactly 100 kè. Cycles, orbits and oscillations finally share the same unit with the calendar.
geometry.trigTitle: And a new era of trigonometry.

heritage.title: Not a new idea. We finished it.
heritage.lead: Great civilizations have long tried to divide the day more sensibly. Nu:Time borrows their wisdom and adds what none of them had: a planet that can agree on the same moment — no matter where you are.

items.title: The kè (刻)
items.text: For more than two thousand years, Chinese astronomers divided the day into 100 kè, measured by water clocks — the same kè at the heart of Nu:Time. Night was kept in five watches, the gēng (更). The Nu:Time Standard · 刻时 Ke-Shi restores the gēng (更) and kè (刻) to their rightful spot.

items.title: The decimal Revolution
items.text: Revolutionary France made the day 10 hours, 100 minutes, and 100 seconds — exactly the same as the Nu:Time gong, beat and tick. Metres and kilograms conquered the world; decimal time was just too early.

items.title: A whole country in the wrong time zone
items.text: Spain sits mostly west of Greenwich yet adopted Central European Time, in 1940. Its clocks still run an hour or more ahead of its sun — a living example of what time zones do to daily life.

why.title: Why now.
why.lead: The measurement of time is now being rebuilt from the atom up, yet the display of time has not changed since Babylon. It's time.

items.title: The second is being redefined
items.text: Optical atomic clocks now outperform the caesium clocks that define the SI second. Metrologists are on a roadmap to redefine the second around 2030. If the foundation is being replaced, the façade can be too.

items.title: Leap seconds were always the problem
items.text: UTC fixes the day at 86,400 atomic seconds, so it has had to insert 27 leap seconds since 1972 to keep up with the Earth — and by 2035 leap seconds will end, letting civil time drift away from the sun. Nu:Time aligns to the Earth's actual turn, so it never needs another leap second. That's how we know the time is now.

items.title: Time zones are politics, not physics
items.text: Dozens of offsets are in use worldwide. China spans five time zones on one clock. India spans nearly two. Spain is shifted an entire hour. Nu:Time separates the shared time from the local sun.

items.title: Daylight saving has lost the argument
items.text: Twice a year, a billion people break their sleep for a 1916 energy policy. The European Parliament voted in 2019 to end seasonal clock changes; the clocks are still changing. Nu:Time has no daylight saving to abolish.

items.title: Machines don't need base 60
items.text: Satellites, payment rails, sensors and AI agents coordinate across every zone at once. Base 60 is a translation layer they tolerate. A decimal day is simply easier to compute.

items.title: Towards 2035: the world's next standards are being written
items.text: China is actively shaping international standards in emerging technology, and its BeiDou Navigation Satellite System and the National Time Service Center of the Chinese Academy of Sciences are now important forces in how the world keeps time. 刻时 Ke-Shi — rooted in ancient China's hundred-kè day — is offered as an open standard for that work, and for everyone.

build.title: Open. Build one.
build.lead: Nu:Time Standard · 刻时 Ke-Shi is an open standard. The specification and reference implementations are free for anyone to use, and build and ship with — the standard belongs to everyone and the Nu:Time · 刻时 Ke-Shi name stands for precision.

items.title: The Standard v1.0
items.text: Units, kè, universal synchronization, latitude and longitude, the 100-kè circle, solar position and the nu-time/v1 record. CC BY 4.0.

items.title: APIs: JavaScript & Python
items.text: Drop-in conversions between UTC and Nu:Time and between degrees and kè, including latitude and longitude — all with shared test vectors. MIT or Apache 2.0.

items.title: Open hardware clock
items.text: A reference design: low-power ARM MCU, GNSS for UTC and kè coordinates, MIP display, and a haptic pulse every kè. CERN-OHL-P 2.0.
